claim: Social behaviour is regulated by activity of host-associated microbiota across multiple species.
source: Social behaviour is regulated by activity of host-associated microbiota across multiple species.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by citations throughout the manuscript to multiple studies across species.

claim: In GF mice the dynamic response seen in controls was attenuated and replaced by a marked increase in expression of splicing factors and alternative exon usage upon stimulation.
source: In GF mice the dynamic response seen in controls was attenuated and replaced by a marked increase in expression of splicing factors and alternative exon usage in GF mice upon stimulation, which was even more pronounced in exGF mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript showing differential gene expression and alternative splicing patterns.

claim: The increase in expression of splicing factors and alternative exon usage was even more pronounced in exGF mice.
source: In GF mice the dynamic response seen in controls was attenuated and replaced by a marked increase in expression of splicing factors and alternative exon usage in GF mice upon stimulation, which was even more pronounced in exGF mice.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing GF and exGF mice.

claim: Social behaviour is correlated with the gene-expression response in the amygdala, established during neurodevelopment as a result of host-microbe interactions.
source: Our data further suggest that social behaviour is correlated with the gene-expression response in the amygdala, established during neurodevelopment as a result of host-microbe interactions.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between behavioral performance and gene expression shown in Figure 5.

claim: Host neurodevelopment, brain function and behaviour are regulated by presence and activity of the host-associated microbiota.
source: Although we only very recently started to understand the intimate relationship between microbes and host physiology, including brain function, it is now well accepted that host neurodevelopment, brain function and behaviour are regulated by presence and activity of the host-associated microbiota (Collins et al., 2012; Cryan and Dinan, 2012; Foster et al., 2017; Lyte, 2013; Mayer et al., 2014a; Sampson and Mazmanian, 2015; Sharon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Host social behaviour is one of the most recurrent and evolutionary conserved behaviours observed to be influenced by the microbiota.
source: One of the most recurrent and evolutionary conserved behaviours observed to be influenced by the microbiota, both during a host's lifetime as well as on evolutionary time scales, is host social behaviour (Arentsen et al., 2015; Crumeyrolle-Arias et al., 2014; de Theije et al., 2014; Desbonnet et al., 2014; Ezenwa et al., 2012; Gacias et al., 2016; Kwong et al., 2017; Leclaire et al., 2017; Lewin-Epstein et al., 2017; Montiel-Castro et al., 2013; Montiel-Castro et al., 2014; Parashar and Udayabanu, 2016; Sharon et al., 2010; Snyder-Mackler et al., 2016; Stilling et al., 2014a; Theis et al., 2013; Tung et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to prior research across multiple species.

claim: A growing body of data in healthy volunteers and patient populations indicates microbial influences translate to human emotional behaviours.
source: Importantly, a growing body of data in healthy volunteers and patient populations is emerging, indicating microbial influences also translate to human emotional behaviours (Tillisch et al., 2013) and have been suggested to play a role in neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) (Stilling et al., 2014a; Hsiao et al., 2013; Kang et al., 2017; Mayer et al., 2014b; Strati et al., 2017) and schizophrenia (Dinan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in human populations.

claim: The microbiota is necessary for expression of autistic-like symptoms in two independent mouse models of autism.
source: Just very recently, it was shown in two independent mouse models of autism that the microbiota is necessary for expression of autistic-like symptoms in these models (Golubeva et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two recent studies.

claim: The amygdala is critically involved in anxiety and fear-related behaviours and memory.
source: While the amygdala is critically involved in anxiety and fear-related behaviours and memory, it is also a well-established key emotional brain centre for evaluating and responding to social stimuli in humans and other mammals (Allsop et al., 2014; Amaral, 2003; Kliemann et al., 2012; Noonan et al., 2014; Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Sabatini et al., 2007; Sallet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: The amygdala is a well-established key emotional brain centre for evaluating and responding to social stimuli in humans and other mammals.
source: While the amygdala is critically involved in anxiety and fear-related behaviours and memory, it is also a well-established key emotional brain centre for evaluating and responding to social stimuli in humans and other mammals (Allsop et al., 2014; Amaral, 2003; Kliemann et al., 2012; Noonan et al., 2014; Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Sabatini et al., 2007; Sallet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: Neuropsychiatric disorders characterised by social deficits (including autism spectrum and anxiety disorders) are associated with structural and functional changes in the amygdala.
source: As such, neuropsychiatric disorders characterised by social deficits (including autism spectrum and anxiety disorders) are associated with structural and functional changes in the amygdala (Amaral and Corbett, 2003; Baron-Cohen et al., 2000; Monk et al., 2010; Schultz, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical neuroscience literature.

claim: Evidence for a role of the microbiota in regulating amygdala function is emerging.
source: Evidence for a role of the microbiota in regulating amygdala function is emerging (Tillisch et al., 2013; Hoban et al., 2018; Stilling et al., 2015; Luczynski et al., 2016a; Hoban et al., 2017) but this has been largely descriptive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Germ-free (GF) mice, lacking microbial colonisation throughout development, are a well-established and essential tool for characterising microbiota-host interactions.
source: Germ-free (GF) mice, lacking microbial colonisation throughout development, are a well-established and essential tool spearheading the characterisation of microbiota-host interactions in regulating development and physiological and behavioural parameters in the host (Desbonnet et al., 2014; Hsiao et al., 2013; Bäckhed et al., 2007; Bercik et al., 2011; Clarke et al., 2013; Diaz Heijtz et al., 2011; McVey Neufeld et al., 2013; Neufeld et al., 2011; Ridaura et al., 2013; Luczynski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior GF mouse studies.

claim: By colonising GF mice at weaning age (exGF), developmental effects can be distinguished from dynamic, reversible effects of a functional microbiota.
source: By colonising GF mice at weaning age (exGF), developmental effects can be distinguished from dynamic, reversible effects of a functional microbiota.
evidence: This is a methodological statement based on established experimental approaches.

claim: Previous studies on post-weaning colonisation of formerly GF rodents have produced mixed results with some phenotypes being reversible while others seemed to be developmentally programmed.
source: Previous studies, focussed on the ability of post-weaning colonisation of formerly GF rodents to reverse behavioural deficits, have produced mixed results with some phenotypes being reversible while others seemed to be developmentally programmed (see (Stilling et al., 2014b) for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The microbiota is a critical regulator of social interaction-induced gene expression in the amygdala.
source: We here provide evidence that the microbiota is a critical regulator of social interaction-induced gene expression in the amygdala.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: GF mice display a unique transcriptional response that involves upregulation of the splicing machinery.
source: We find a unique transcriptional response in GF mice that involves upregulation of the splicing machinery, which is able to partially compensate for impairments in neuronal plasticity signalling during social interaction in these animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq data and functional enrichment analysis.

claim: The upregulation of the splicing machinery in GF mice is able to partially compensate for impairments in neuronal plasticity signalling during social interaction.
source: We find a unique transcriptional response in GF mice that involves upregulation of the splicing machinery, which is able to partially compensate for impairments in neuronal plasticity signalling during social interaction in these animals.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the observed data patterns.

claim: Mice lacking any interaction with microorganisms throughout development have a range of behavioural phenotypes.
source: Mice lacking any interaction with microorganisms throughout development have a range of behavioural phenotypes (Luczynski et al., 2016), including memory impairments and altered anxiety behaviour (Hoban et al., 2018; Gareau et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: GF mice show significantly decreased interaction with a conspecific compared with controls and colonized animals.
source: As previously reported (Desbonnet et al., 2014; Buffington et al., 2016), on average the group of GF-SI mice showed significantly decreased interaction with a conspecific compared with controls and colonized animals, while interaction with the non-social object was similar among the three groups (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B-C and citations to prior studies.

claim: Interaction with the non-social object was similar among the three groups (CON, GF, exGF).
source: As previously reported (Desbonnet et al., 2014; Buffington et al., 2016), on average the group of GF-SI mice showed significantly decreased interaction with a conspecific compared with controls and colonized animals, while interaction with the non-social object was similar among the three groups (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: There was high inter-individual variability in the GF-SI group for the time interacting with the conspecific, ranging from approximately control levels (>300 s) to as little as 60 s.
source: Notably, we found high inter-individual variability in the GF-SI group for the time interacting with the conspecific, ranging from approximately control levels (>300 s) to as little as 60 s (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The distribution of social interaction time in GF-SI mice passed the D'Agostino and Pearson omnibus normality test, the Shapiro-Wilk normality test and the KS normality test, all at alpha = 0.05.
source: However, the distribution passed the D'Agostino and Pearson omnibus normality test, the Shapiro-Wilk normality test and the KS normality test, all at alpha = 0.05.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Time spent with the non-social object was similarly variable in all three groups.
source: Time spent with the non-social object was similarly variable in all three groups (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Social interactions in the mouse 3CSIT behavioural paradigm reliably activates stimulus-dependent genes expression in the amygdala.
source: Since we have previously shown that social interactions in the mouse 3CSIT behavioural paradigm reliably activates stimulus-dependent genes expression in the amygdala (Stilling et al., 2015), we hypothesised that we would observe changes in gene expression in this brain region as a function of colonisation status and, especially, social experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: The highest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in naïve animals was found in the CON-GF comparison.
source: When comparing the number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs, both up- and downregulated) between naïve animals of different colonisation status, we find the highest number of DEGs in the CON-GF comparison (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1), as we have previously reported in an independent study (Stilling et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and citation to a prior study.

claim: When comparing naïve vs. stimulated animals the response in terms of number of DEGs was strongest in GF animals by far.
source: Interestingly, when comparing naïve vs. stimulated animals the response in terms of number of DEGs was strongest in GF animals by far, providing evidence for the amygdalar transcriptomes to diverge between the three groups upon environmental stimulation by social interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transcriptional divergence driven by neuronal activity is supported by the number of DEGs when comparing the SI groups among each other, as these numbers are substantially (4–9 times) higher than DEG numbers for naïve comparisons.
source: Transcriptional divergence driven by neuronal activity is further supported by the number of DEGs when comparing the SI groups among each other, as these numbers are substantially (4–9 times) higher than DEG numbers for naïve comparisons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a core cluster of genes that are induced 1 hr after social novelty, independent of colonisation status.
source: As expected, there were multiple overlapping clusters between SI comparisons, demonstrating a core cluster of genes that are induced 1 hr after social novelty, independent of colonisation status.
evidence: This claim is supported by the presence-absence plot shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A cluster of genes was differentially regulated in both GF naïve animals and upon social interaction stimulation in conventional animals.
source: We identified a cluster of genes that was differentially regulated in both GF naïve animals and upon social interaction stimulation in conventional animals (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The overlap between genes differentially regulated in GF naïve animals and upon social interaction stimulation in conventional animals was highly significant and made up large proportions of all genes up- or downregulated in naive GF animals compared to CON controls (38% and 26%, respectively).
source: This overlap was highly significant and made up large proportions of all genes up- or downregulated in naive GF animals compared to CON controls (38% and 26%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the overlap shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The cluster of genes differentially regulated in both GF naïve animals and upon social interaction stimulation in conventional animals was not differentially regulated in GF animals upon stimulation by social interaction.
source: This cluster was not differentially regulated in GF animals upon stimulation by social interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Several genes typically induced in the amygdala of conventional controls upon social interaction are already elevated in GF mice, pointing towards amygdalar hyperactivity in these animals.
source: Together, these data suggest that several genes typically induced in the amygdala of conventional controls upon social interaction are already elevated in GF mice, pointing towards amygdalar hyperactivity in these animals (Stilling et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the overlap data and supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: For all three groups (CON-SI, GF-SI, exGF-SI) significant enrichment was found for processes such as protein modification and folding as well as regulation of gene expression.
source: For all three groups significant enrichment was found for processes such as protein modification and folding as well as regulation of gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Processes associated with intracellular signalling such as protein phosphorylation and dephosphorylation were enriched in the CON-SI comparison, but not in GF-SI or exGF-SI.
source: However, large differences were seen in processes that are associated with intracellular signalling such as protein phosphorylation and dephosphorylation, which was enriched in the CON-SI comparison, but not in GF-SI or exGF-SI.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Processes associated with RNA splicing were dramatically enriched most prominently in the GF-SI but also the exGF-SI group.
source: The second striking difference was dramatic enrichment of processes associated with RNA splicing, most prominently in the GF-SI but also the exGF-SI group (Figure 2E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In the CON-SI group the MAP kinase (MAPK) signalling pathway was the dominant pathway enriched due to social interaction treatment.
source: As expected, in the CON-SI group the MAP kinase (MAPK) signalling pathway was the dominant pathway enriched due to social interaction treatment (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The MAPK signalling pathway was also enriched in GF-SI and exGI-SI groups, albeit to a much lesser degree than in CON-SI.
source: This pathway, which is well established to be induced upon neuronal activity, was also enriched in GF-SI and exGI-SI groups, albeit to a much lesser degree.
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For the GF-SI group there was a highly significant enrichment of genes associated with the spliceosome.
source: For the GF-SI group we found a highly significant enrichment of genes associated with the spliceosome that was also significantly enriched, to a lesser extent, in the exGF-SI group and almost completely absent from the CON-SI group (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Genes associated with the spliceosome were also significantly enriched in the exGF-SI group, to a lesser extent than in GF-SI.
source: For the GF-SI group we found a highly significant enrichment of genes associated with the spliceosome that was also significantly enriched, to a lesser extent, in the exGF-SI group and almost completely absent from the CON-SI group (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Genes associated with the spliceosome were almost completely absent from the CON-SI group.
source: For the GF-SI group we found a highly significant enrichment of genes associated with the spliceosome that was also significantly enriched, to a lesser extent, in the exGF-SI group and almost completely absent from the CON-SI group (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: DEGs exclusively upregulated in CON-SI mice were highly enriched in genes involved in intracellular signalling, especially the MAPK pathway.
source: In line with GO Term and KEGG pathway analysis we found that DEGs exclusively upregulated in CON-SI mice, were highly enriched in genes involved in intracellular signalling, especially the MAPK pathway, while DEGs exclusively upregulated in GF-SI mice were strongly enriched in genes associated with RNA processing, that is splicing (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DEGs exclusively upregulated in GF-SI mice were strongly enriched in genes associated with RNA processing, that is splicing.
source: In line with GO Term and KEGG pathway analysis we found that DEGs exclusively upregulated in CON-SI mice, were highly enriched in genes involved in intracellular signalling, especially the MAPK pathway, while DEGs exclusively upregulated in GF-SI mice were strongly enriched in genes associated with RNA processing, that is splicing (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The core of genes that are induced independent of colonisation status is characterised by enrichment of genes involved in protein folding and, to a lesser degree, both, spliceosome and MAPK signalling pathway.
source: The core of genes that are induced independent of colonisation status is characterised by enrichment of genes involved in protein folding and, to a lesser degree, both, spliceosome and MAPK signalling pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of overlapping genes.

claim: Genes associated with the GO Term 'RNA processing' made up 4.4% of all DEGs in the GF-SI group (111/2510), which represents 15% of all mouse genes in this category (111/741).
source: Genes associated with the GO Term 'RNA processing' made up 4.4% of all DEGs in the GF-SI group (111/2510), which represents 15% of all mouse genes in this category (111/741).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Expression of RNA processing genes is highly distinctive in GF-SI animals when comparing response-induced fold changes between colonisation statuses.
source: Comparing response-induced fold changes of these 111 genes between colonisation statuses, further highlighted that expression of this group of genes is highly distinctive in GF-SI animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Stimulus-induced upregulation of a number of well-established immediate early genes was seen in the amygdala of conventional animals after social interaction.
source: Stimulus-induced upregulation of a number of well-established immediate early genes, that show rapid and reproducible upregulation in response to neuronal activity, including activity induced by environmental novelty in the hippocampus, was also seen in the amygdala of conventional animals after social interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Several immediate early genes, including Egr3, Fos, and Ier5, were not upregulated in GF-SI mice, possibly due to elevated expression levels at baseline.
source: In line with reduced activation of the MAPK pathway in GF-SI mice, we find several of these genes, including Egr3, Fos, and Ier5 not to be upregulated in this group, possibly due to elevated expression levels at baseline (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential gene expression data and is an inference about the mechanism.

claim: GF animals show a unique response signature toward environmental stimulation by social interaction characterised by a marked upregulation of the genes involved in RNA processing and the splicing machinery, accompanied by an arrested upregulation of typical response genes, especially in those involved in MAPK signalling.
source: Together these data suggest that GF animals show a unique response signature toward environmental stimulation by social interaction. The transcriptional response is characterised by a marked upregulation of the genes involved in RNA processing and the splicing machinery, accompanied by an arrested upregulation of typical response genes, especially in those involved in MAPK signalling.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple lines of evidence from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Analysis of differential gene expression between naïve GF animals and controls revealed that lack of induction of certain genes may be due to upregulation of several genes involved in these processes already at baseline.
source: Analysis of differential gene expression between naïve GF animals and controls also revealed that this lack of induction may be due to upregulation of several genes involved in these processes already at baseline.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the differential gene expression data.

claim: All analyses on GF animals colonised with a conventional microbiota at weaning (exGF) show results with features of both, CON and GF groups.
source: All analyses on GF animals colonised with a conventional microbiota at weaning (exGF) presented so far show results with features of both, CON and GF groups.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Under naïve conditions alternative splicing was highest when comparing CON and GF animals.
source: Under naïve conditions alternative splicing was highest when comparing CON and GF animals (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential splicing analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Differentially spliced genes (DSGs) between CON and GF naïve animals were highly enriched in several functional categories involved in neuronal function, such as long-term potentiation (padj = 2.3e-6) and synaptic transmission (padj = 1.2e-10).
source: These genes were highly enriched in several functional categories involved in neuronal function, such as long-term potentiation (padj = 2.3e-6) and synaptic transmission (padj = 1.2e-10) (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of DSGs.

claim: High congruence in alternative splicing between CON and exGF mice was evident from the high degree of overlap between DSGs that distinguished both groups from the GF group.
source: High congruence in alternative splicing between CON and exGF mice was also evident from the high degree of overlap between DSGs that distinguished both groups from the GF group (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Conventionally colonised controls exposed to social interaction showed comparatively little alternative exon usage.
source: While conventionally colonised controls exposed to social interaction showed comparatively little alternative exon usage, we found a dramatically increased number of DSGs in the GF-SI group, and noticed an even higher number of SI-induced DSGs in exGF animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential splicing analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was a dramatically increased number of DSGs in the GF-SI group.
source: While conventionally colonised controls exposed to social interaction showed comparatively little alternative exon usage, we found a dramatically increased number of DSGs in the GF-SI group, and noticed an even higher number of SI-induced DSGs in exGF animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential splicing analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was an even higher number of SI-induced DSGs in exGF animals than in GF animals.
source: While conventionally colonised controls exposed to social interaction showed comparatively little alternative exon usage, we found a dramatically increased number of DSGs in the GF-SI group, and noticed an even higher number of SI-induced DSGs in exGF animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential splicing analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The finding that enrichment of splicing-associated genes among DEGs was highest in the GF-SI comparison was surprising given that the number of SI-induced DSGs was even higher in exGF animals.
source: This was surprising since enrichment of splicing-associated genes among DEGs was highest in the GF-SI comparison, albeit significantly present also in the exGF-SI group.
evidence: This is an observation about the unexpected relationship between two findings.

claim: DSGs of the three comparisons (CON-SI, GF-SI, exGF-SI) shared a 'core' set of genes that were alternatively spliced in response to social interaction, independent of colonisation status.
source: As with the previous finding for DEGs, DSGs of the three comparisons also shared a 'core' set of genes that were alternatively spliced in response to social interaction, independent of colonisation status (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The core set of DSGs shared across colonisation statuses was slightly enriched in genes associated with functional categories involved in neuronal function such as long-term potentiation (padj=1.5e-02) and synaptic transmission (padj=1.9e-4).
source: This core was slightly enriched in genes associated with functional categories that are involved in neuronal function such as long-term potentiation (padj=1.5e-02) and synaptic transmission (padj=1.9e-4).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of the core DSGs.

claim: In addition to the conventional response, GF-SI and exGF-SI groups show supplementary cellular responses towards activation of the amygdala by social interaction.
source: In fact, the high degree of overlap between all three groups together with the high number of DSGs in GF-SI and exGF-SI groups suggests that, in addition to the conventional response, these two groups show supplementary cellular responses towards activation of the amygdala by social interaction.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the DSG overlap and enrichment data.

claim: The additional response in exGF-SI mice is even more pronounced than in GF-SI mice and is characterised by a high number of DSGs highly enriched in genes involved in mainly four principal functional categories: splicing/RNA processing, protein turnover, neuronal functions, and intracellular signalling pathways.
source: Interestingly, this additional response is even more pronounced in the exGF-SI group and is characterised by a high number of DSGs highly enriched in genes involved in mainly four principal functional categories: splicing/RNA processing, protein turnover, neuronal functions, and intracellular signalling pathways (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A highly enriched proportion of the alternatively spliced genes themselves were also members of the splicing machinery, suggesting a self-regulating mechanism of gene expression in GF-SI and exGF-SI groups.
source: The fact that a highly enriched proportion of the alternatively spliced genes themselves were also members of the splicing machinery suggests a self-regulating mechanism of gene expression in these two groups.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the functional enrichment data.

claim: Genes whose expression was positively correlated with social interaction time in GF-SI mice were significantly associated with splicing, along with protein turnover.
source: Excitingly, genes whose expression was positively correlated with social interaction time were significantly associated with splicing, along with protein turnover (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: There was no significant gene set enrichment for negative correlations between sociability behaviour and gene expression in GF-SI mice.
source: There was no significant gene set enrichment for negative correlations between sociability behaviour and gene expression.
evidence: This is a negative result from the GSEA analysis.

claim: The correlation between expression of splicing and protein turnover genes and behavioral performance suggests direct involvement of these pathways in the amygdala with behavioural performance.
source: These data suggest direct involvement of splicing and protein turnover pathways in the amygdala with behavioural performance.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the correlation analysis.

claim: Three genes (DnaJb6, Cribp, and D030028A08Rik) were significantly higher expressed in GF-SIhigh animals compared to GF-SIlow animals.
source: We found three genes that were significantly higher expressed in GF-SIhigh animals, namely DnaJb6 (encoding a brain-enriched heat-shock family protein with chaperone function), Cribp (encoding a stimulus-inducible, brain-enriched, nuclear RNA-binding protein involved in mRNA stabilization), and D030028A08Rik (a long-noncoding RNA with yet unknown function).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis within the GF-SI group.

claim: DnaJb6, Cribp, and D030028A08Rik show a statistically significant correlation with behavioural performance in the GF-SI group.
source: These three genes also show a statistically significant correlation with behavioural performance in the GF-SI group (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The amygdala is a key node in the emotional processing network, responsible for processing social stimuli and fear-related cues.
source: The amygdala is a key node in the emotional processing network, responsible for processing social stimuli and fear-related cues (Allsop et al., 2014; Amaral, 2003; Kliemann et al., 2012; Noonan et al., 2014; Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Sabatini et al., 2007; Sallet et al., 2011; Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: A rapidly developing literature increasingly implicates the microbiome in host brain function and behaviour, especially in emotion processing networks.
source: A rapidly developing literature increasingly implicates the microbiome in host brain function and behaviour, especially in these emotion processing networks (Crumeyrolle-Arias et al., 2014; Luczynski et al., 2016a; Clarke et al., 2013; Diaz Heijtz et al., 2011; Neufeld et al., 2011; Arseneault-Bréard et al., 2012; Bercik et al., 2010; Gilbert et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Social behaviour appears to be among the behaviours most intimately connected to a functional microbiome.
source: Social behaviour appears to be among the behaviours most intimately connected to a functional microbiome (Arentsen et al., 2015; Desbonnet et al., 2014; Gacias et al., 2016; Lewin-Epstein et al., 2017; Theis et al., 2013; Tung et al., 2015; Hsiao et al., 2013; Buffington et al., 2016; Arentsen et al., 2017; Koch and Schmid-Hempel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Absence of the microbiome results in dysregulation of unique transcriptional-response pathways in the amygdala.
source: Here we show, for what is to our knowledge the first time, that absence of the microbiome results in dysregulation of unique transcriptional-response pathways in the amygdala.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: Microbes are necessary for development of appropriate sociability behaviour.
source: In line with previous reports, we show that microbes are necessary for development of appropriate sociability behaviour (Arentsen et al., 2015; Desbonnet et al., 2014; Buffington et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data and citations to prior studies.

claim: Reduced sociability behaviour of GF mice in the three-chamber social interaction task is rescued by post-weaning colonisation with a conventional microbiome.
source: In agreement with these studies we show reduced sociability behaviour of GF mice in the three-chamber social interaction task, rescued by post-weaning colonisation with a conventional microbiome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: GF mice do not show a lack of preference of the conspecific mouse over an inanimate novel object.
source: However, we do not observe a lack of preference of the conspecific mouse over an inanimate novel object in GF mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The underlying networks controlling sociability behaviour are subject to a dynamic regulation, possibly associated with differences in intracellular and extracellular neuronal signalling pathways due to subtle differences accumulating during individual development.
source: This finding suggests, that the underlying networks controlling sociability behaviour are subject to a dynamic regulation, possibly associated with differences in intracellular and extracellular neuronal signalling pathways due to subtle differences accumulating during individual development.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed behavioral variability.

claim: The development of networks controlling sociability behaviour is highly susceptible to influence by symbiotic signals from the microbiota.
source: However, the fact that exGF mice, colonised with a conventional microbiota at weaning age, spent an intermediate amount of time in social interaction with more control-like variability within the group, argues that this development is highly susceptible to influence by symbiotic signals from the microbiota.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the behavioral data for exGF mice.

claim: In several analyses of gene expression regulation in response to social interaction exGF mice resemble an intermediate phenotype, bearing features of both CON and GF mice.
source: Also in several analyses of gene expression regulation in response to social interaction exGF mice resemble an intermediate phenotype, bearing features of both CON and GF mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study used stranded, ribodepleted as opposed to poly-A enriched libraries for RNA-sequencing to characterize real transcriptome-wide changes in gene expression.
source: To characterize real transcriptome-wide changes in gene expression, in this study we used stranded, ribodepleted as opposed to poly-A enriched libraries for RNA-sequencing.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.

claim: The study describes dynamic regulation of several previously undescribed pathways in response to environmental stimulation, including regulation of RNA-processing non-coding RNAs.
source: In result, we describe dynamic regulation of several previously undescribed pathways in response to environmental stimulation. As such, we see regulation of RNA-processing non-coding RNAs, several of which are found in subnuclear Cajal bodies, that are particularly prominent in neurons - especially, when transcriptionally active - and are crucially involved in splicing regulation (Wang et al., 2016; Lafarga et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data and citations to literature on Cajal bodies.

claim: Induction of gene expression in the amygdala shows similarities with the hippocampal transcriptional response to environmental novelty.
source: Interestingly, induction of gene expression in this brain region shows similarities with the hippocampal transcriptional response to environmental novelty (Stilling et al., 2014c).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with a prior study cited.

claim: The overlap between amygdala and hippocampal transcriptional responses is very likely due to a ubiquitous, though highly specific transcriptional response in neurons towards neuronal activity.
source: This overlap is very likely due to a ubiquitous, though highly specific transcriptional response in neurons towards neuronal activity, which includes induction of several well established immediate early genes such as Fos or Arc, the MAP-K pathway, and neurotrophic signalling via Bdnf.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the observed overlap and established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: The study found upregulation of complement components upon social interaction in CON mice.
source: Moreover, we find upregulation of complement components, which have lately been established to be necessary for synaptic rearrangements and plasticity upon neuronal activity (Schafer et al., 2012; Stephan et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data and citations to literature on complement function.

claim: Innate immune system genes together with neuronal activity-dependent genes have recently been shown to be dysregulated in autism.
source: Interestingly, innate immune system genes together with neuronal activity-dependent genes have recently been shown to be dysregulated in autism (Gupta et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Induction of complement genes upon social interaction was not seen in GF mice, possibly due to upregulation of C1q already under naïve conditions as compared to CON mice.
source: Induction of complement genes upon social interaction was not seen in GF mice, possibly due to upregulation of C1q already under naïve conditions as compared to CON mice.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: Altered splicing activity is a normal process in neurons of the amygdala in response to social interaction in conventionally raised mice.
source: Our data further shows that altered splicing activity is a normal process in neurons of the amygdala in response to social interaction in conventionally raised mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential splicing analysis.

claim: Neuronal activity induces alternative splicing patterns.
source: Indeed, it is now well established, that neuronal activity induces alternative splicing patterns (Ding et al., 2017; Hermey et al., 2017; Iijima et al., 2016; Schor et al., 2009), a dysfunction of which has been associated with changes seen in autism and autistic-like behaviour in mice (Quesnel-Vallières et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Dysfunction of alternative splicing has been associated with changes seen in autism and autistic-like behaviour in mice.
source: Indeed, it is now well established, that neuronal activity induces alternative splicing patterns (Ding et al., 2017; Hermey et al., 2017; Iijima et al., 2016; Schor et al., 2009), a dysfunction of which has been associated with changes seen in autism and autistic-like behaviour in mice (Quesnel-Vallières et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The regulation of genes involved in splicing, including Cajal body-associated genes, as well as alternative splicing activity is extremely exaggerated in GF mice, which possibly reflects a compensatory mechanism for already elevated activity-induced signalling at baseline.
source: Surprisingly, the regulation of genes involved in splicing, including Cajal body-associated genes, as well as alternative splicing activity is extremely exaggerated in GF mice, which possibly reflects a compensatory mechanism for already elevated activity-induced signalling at baseline.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the observed data patterns.

claim: Increased splicing activity is even more amplified in exGF mice, which display a largely normalized behavioural response.
source: The finding that increased splicing activity is even more amplified in exGF mice, which display a largely normalized behavioural response, together with a positive correlation between expression of splicing-associated genes and behavioural performance suggests that in fact upregulation of the splicing machinery supports an adequate amygdalar response towards a social interaction environmental stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential splicing data and behavioral data.

claim: The positive correlation between expression of splicing-associated genes and behavioural performance suggests that upregulation of the splicing machinery supports an adequate amygdalar response towards a social interaction environmental stimulus.
source: The finding that increased splicing activity is even more amplified in exGF mice, which display a largely normalized behavioural response, together with a positive correlation between expression of splicing-associated genes and behavioural performance suggests that in fact upregulation of the splicing machinery supports an adequate amygdalar response towards a social interaction environmental stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the correlation analysis and behavioral data.

claim: Previous research shows that post-weaning colonization (exGF) does not rescue impairments in social cognition, seen in GF mice.
source: In fact, previous research shows that post-weaning colonization (exGF) does not rescue impairments in social cognition, seen in GF mice (Desbonnet et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The incomplete rescue of social cognition in exGF mice is likely a reflection of an incomplete rescue of the molecular underpinnings of social behaviour.
source: This is likely a reflection of an incomplete rescue of the molecular underpinnings of social behaviour investigated here.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim connecting the behavioral and molecular findings.

claim: The data is fully congruent with and offers a molecular basis for previous data on alterations in social cognition, amygdala volume and dendrite complexity, and increased transcription of activity-associated gene expression in the amygdala in microbiome-deficient mice.
source: In summary, our data is fully congruent with and offers a molecular basis for previous data on alterations in social cognition (Desbonnet et al., 2014), amygdala volume and dendrite complexity (Luczynski et al., 2016a), and increased transcription of activity-associated gene expression in the amygdala (Hoban et al., 2018; Stilling et al., 2015) in microbiome-deficient mice.
evidence: This is a summary claim connecting the current findings to prior literature.

claim: The microbiota is necessary for regulation of core biological processes on the molecular and cellular level in the brain.
source: We here show for what is to our knowledge the first time that the microbiota is necessary for regulation of core biological processes on the molecular and cellular level in the brain, which makes a strong case for a causal involvement of the microbiota in the molecular mechanisms leading to the observed impairments in sociability behaviour and the aetiology of neurodevelopmental diseases, which opens the possibility for new therapeutic strategies.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: The findings make a strong case for a causal involvement of the microbiota in the molecular mechanisms leading to the observed impairments in sociability behaviour and the aetiology of neurodevelopmental diseases.
